documents.title: Why small airports are fighting to survive
documents.text:
Regional airports, once a symbol of civic pride, are struggling across the continent. Passenger numbers at many have not recovered to the levels seen before the pandemic, and several airlines have withdrawn routes that they judge to be unprofitable, leaving terminals that handle a few flights a day and employ far more staff than the traffic requires.

Local officials argue that such airports are more than commercial ventures. They connect remote communities to the national network, bring in visitors who support hotels and restaurants, and offer a base for emergency services. A study of one island airport estimated that every job at the airport supported two more in the surrounding economy.

Economists are less sentimental. They point out that subsidies to keep airports open, which in some cases exceed the revenue they generate, could be spent on rail links or road improvements that serve more people. They also note that low-cost carriers, which have the power to open or close routes, extract concessions from airports by threatening to leave, a bargaining position that leaves smaller operators with little leverage.

Some airports have found a different path. One has converted unused hangars into a training center for pilots and engineers, and another has become a testing site for electric aircraft. Neither has yet replaced the lost revenue from scheduled flights, but both suggest that survival may depend on finding a new purpose.

choices: Low-cost airlines are opening many new routes

questions.explanation: They extract concessions by threatening to leave.

choices: They have saved every airport that has tried them

questions.explanation: Neither has yet replaced the lost revenue from scheduled flights.

documents.title: Following up on an unanswered supplier query
documents.text:
To: Hiroshi Tanabe, Account Manager, Kestrel Packaging
From: Louisa Brandt, Purchasing, Marlowe Foods
Subject: Second request: revised pricing for the autumn range

Dear Mr. Tanabe,

I wrote to you on 2 September to ask for revised pricing on the cartons for our autumn range, and I have not yet had a reply. I understand that this is a busy period, and I do not wish to suggest negligence, but our own deadline is approaching and I must ask for a response by Friday.

The reason for the urgency is that our packaging contract with Kestrel expires at the end of the month, and we must decide by 20 September whether to renew or to seek bids elsewhere. In July you indicated that a price increase of around four percent was likely; I should like to know whether this remains your intention, since a larger rise would make a competing offer attractive.

I should add that we value the relationship, which has lasted six years, and that we have been satisfied with the quality and punctuality of your deliveries. The difficulty is purely one of cost. If Kestrel can hold the price at the current level for a further year, I am confident that we would renew for a longer period.

Please let me know if a call would be easier than an email.

Kind regards,
Louisa Brandt

documents.title: Notice to residents: roof replacement at Thornbury Court
documents.text:
THORNBURY COURT — NOTICE TO RESIDENTS
Roof replacement: access, noise and scaffolding

Following the survey of March, the management company has appointed Stanhope Roofing to replace the roof of all three blocks. Work will begin on Monday 5 August and is expected to last fourteen weeks, subject to the weather.

Scaffolding will be erected around each block in turn, starting with Block A. Residents on the upper floors should expect restricted use of their balconies during the period when scaffolding is in place; balcony furniture should be removed by 2 August, and the contractor cannot accept responsibility for items left behind. Windows may need to be kept closed on days when the roof is being stripped, since dust is likely.

Work hours will be 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. on weekdays only, and noisy operations will not begin before 9 a.m. Anyone who works nights or is otherwise affected by the daytime noise is invited to contact the site manager, Mr. Delgado, who will try to schedule the loudest work for times that cause least disturbance.

The cost will be met from the reserve fund, and no additional levy will be charged this year. A residents' meeting will be held in the community room on 23 July at 7 p.m. to answer questions.

documents.title: Incident report, with supervisor's note
documents.text:
KILBRIDE MANUFACTURING — INCIDENT REPORT
Date: 14 March    Time: 2:35 p.m.    Location: Packing hall, aisle 6
Reported by: Sofia Marchetti (line operator)

Description: While moving a pallet of boxed components with a hand truck, I noticed that the floor near the cooling unit was wet. The wet area was about two meters wide and had no warning sign. I slipped slightly, but did not fall, and the pallet did not tip. I informed my team leader immediately.

Injuries: None. Equipment damaged: None.

Contributing factors (reporter's view): The cooling unit has leaked on at least two previous occasions this month. On both, the floor was dried but the leak was not reported to maintenance.

Supervisor's note (T. Okonkwo, 14 March, 4:10 p.m.): The area was cordoned off at 2:50 p.m. and dried. Maintenance has been called, and an engineer will inspect the unit tomorrow morning. I agree with the reporter's view that earlier leaks were not escalated, and I have reminded the team that any leak must be reported on the day. Should the unit prove faulty, it will be taken out of service until it is repaired.

documents.title: A documentary that asks the right questions
documents.text:
The Last Harvest follows a family of grape growers in the south of France over three seasons, during which a run of poor weather pushes their vineyard to the edge of bankruptcy. It would have been easy for the director, Elodie Martin, to treat this as a lament for a vanishing way of life; instead she presents a business whose owners are as practical as they are sentimental.

The strongest scenes are the quietest. In one, the father and his son argue across the kitchen table about whether to sell a parcel of land, each in turn making a case that is persuasive and incomplete. Martin does not take sides, and the viewer's sympathy shifts with each speech. The cinematography, which at times lingers lovingly over the hills, is less disciplined, and a few shots seem included purely for their beauty.

The film's weakness is its final third, in which a visiting economist is introduced to explain the wider picture. His comments are accurate but arrive too late and sit awkwardly beside the intimacy of what precedes them.

It is nonetheless a thoughtful work, and it leaves its audience with a question rather than an answer: what are we willing to pay to keep a place as it is?

choices: A sentimental lament for rural life in France

A beautiful film that has no real ideas
questions.explanation: The review praises its balance but criticizes the final third.

choices: A family argument over selling land

A tense meeting with the local bank
questions.explanation: The father and son argue about selling a parcel of land.

questions.explanation: Martin does not take sides, and sympathy shifts.

questions.explanation: The visiting economist's comments sit awkwardly beside the intimacy before.

documents.title: Frequently asked questions about the Greenfield community garden
documents.text:
Who can join the Greenfield community garden? Anyone who lives within three kilometers of the site may apply for a plot. If a plot becomes available, it is offered first to people on the waiting list, in order of application. At present, the wait is about eighteen months.

How much does a plot cost? An annual fee of 40 dollars applies for a standard plot of ten square meters. Residents receiving benefits pay half. The fee covers water, shared tools and insurance, but not seeds or plants.

Can I use pesticides? No. The garden is organic, which means that synthetic pesticides and fertilizers are not allowed. Plot holders who break this rule will receive a written warning, and a second offense leads to the loss of the plot.

What if I am away for a long period? Holidays are not a problem, but plots that are left unattended for more than six weeks during the growing season may be reassigned, since the waiting list is long. Please tell the coordinator if you expect to be away, and arrange for a friend to water your plot.

Can I sell what I grow? Produce may be shared with neighbors and given to the food bank, but not sold, as the garden's lease prohibits trading.

documents.title: The long road to a cheaper battery
documents.text:
For a decade, the price of rechargeable batteries has fallen steadily, and manufacturers have grown used to promising that the decline will continue. Recent figures, however, suggest that the easy gains may be over. After falling by more than eighty percent since 2010, the cost per unit of storage rose slightly last year, largely because of higher prices for lithium and cobalt.

Industry analysts point to two sources of relief. The first is a change of chemistry: several firms now produce batteries that use iron phosphate in place of cobalt, which is both cheaper and less vulnerable to supply disruption. The second is recycling, which in principle can recover most of the valuable metals from used cells, though at present only a small proportion of batteries are processed in this way, because collection systems are inadequate.

A third possibility, much discussed, is the so-called solid-state battery, which promises greater capacity and safety. Yet researchers caution that the technology has been "two years away" for more than ten, and that the difficulties of manufacturing at scale are serious.

The effect of all this on consumers will depend on how long the pause lasts. Electric vehicles, which depend on batteries for around a third of their cost, are likely to feel it first.

documents.title: Reference for a former employee
documents.text:
To whom it may concern,

I am pleased to write in support of Ms. Camille Okoye, who worked as a project coordinator in my department from 2019 until her departure last month to relocate abroad with her family. I have been asked to comment on her suitability for a position as an operations manager, and I do so with confidence.

Ms. Okoye joined us when our department was disorganized and often late with its deliverables. Within a year, she had introduced a weekly tracking system that identified delays before they became crises, and by her third year our on-time record had improved from sixty to ninety percent. She achieved this not by insisting on rules but by persuading colleagues that the system would make their work easier, an ability that is rarer than it should be.

I must be honest about one limitation. Ms. Okoye is at her best when working with teams she knows well, and she took some months to find her footing in a new group after our restructuring in 2022. This is not a serious weakness, but a prospective employer should allow her time to settle.

I would gladly employ her again, and I recommend her without reservation.

Yours faithfully,
Dr. Henrik Alvarez, Director of Operations
